items.title: 千问办公押注 Team Agent，企业 AI 的流水线时刻真的来了
items.description: 传说，光明之神巴德尔梦见自己将死，于是，巴德尔的母亲弗丽嘉遍走世间，令万物立下了绝不伤害他的誓言。众神也因此放下心来，甚至还发明了一种新的消遣：轮番向巴德尔投掷武器和石块，看着他毫发无损，来确定他们已经战胜了预言。直到一小枝被遗漏的槲寄生投向巴德尔。光明之神轰然倒下，诸神的黄昏由此拉开序章。 这是北欧神话中巴德尔之死的故事。危险早已被预见，人们也采取了行动，却仍然自欺欺人，把一次次看似成功的演示，当成了问题已经解决的证明 。

items.description: 11 月 10 日消息， Anthropic 昨日（11 月 9 日）官宣推出 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Claude Mythos 5.2， 两款模型基于同一底层模型，前者面向普通用户并内置网络安全与生物安全防护，后者则面向通过审核的网络安全和生命科学机构开放，用于高风险的专业应用。 定价方面，Claude Fable 5.2 每 100 万词元（Token）输入费用为 8 美元（IT 之家注：现汇率约合 53.4 元人民币），每 100 万词元（Token）输出费用为 40 美元（现汇率约合 267.2 元人民币）。作为对比，Claude Fable 5.1 的每 100 万词元输入 / 输出价格分别为 10 美元（现汇率约合 66.8 元人民币）和 50 美元（现汇率约合 334 元人民币）， 按此计算 5.2 版本的 API 调用费用下调 20%。

items.title: 实测 HY4：腾讯最「夯」大模型，离一线还有多远？
items.description: 11 月 4 日，混元 Hy4 正式发布，模型权重将在近期开源，主打性价比的轻量版 Hy4 flash 也一起亮相。腾讯给它的定位是——首次跻身最强开源模型之列。 过去一年，腾讯在 AI 上最多被人看见的，是 WorkBuddy 这类 Agent 和应用产品；到了更底层的模型上，它的声量明显弱于应用。Hy4 真正要回答的，是腾讯在模型这条线上的身位。

items.description: 11 月 9 日消息，英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋当地时间 8 日于公司官网发布致全员公开信，就个人私事致歉，同时披露董事会将针对相关报道提及的国家安全关切展开独立调查。 黄仁勋在信中承认自己对妻子不忠，坦言该行为伤害家人，对此承担全部责任，并接受外界批评。他表示家人不应为其个人选择负责，恳请公众给予家人隐私空间，希望能有机会重新赢回家人信任。他强调自己对英伟达始终坚定，将努力重新赢得团队与投资方的信赖。

items.title: 为什么「陪伴」，注定是 Personal AI 的核心
items.description: 最近这一波 Personal AI 实在太火了，我也注册了一个 Muse 体验了一下。 整个体验下来，我感觉 Muse 的能力实在一般，远没到让人惊叹的地步。但奇怪的是，它确实带来了一种真切的陪伴感。这种陪伴感，甚至直接改变了我的使用习惯，让我总是忍不住想找它聊聊，哪怕只是把最琐碎的需求丢给它。

items.title: 创业者做 Personal Agent，有没有一线生机？
items.description: 最近一阶段，Personal Agent 很热。有趣的是，这个概念迅速火爆又迅速有了一个共识，几波讨论下来大家的观点似乎是： Personal Agent 的机会是大厂的，创业者基本没戏。 虽然一般情况下，「入口级机会归大厂」确实是大概率发生的事情，但 Personal Agent 真的是个「入口」的问题吗？真的意味着「这件事里没有创业者的位置」吗？

items.title: 办公提效之后，企业级 Agent 开始对经营结果负责
items.description: 从查资料、写文档到处理日常办公事务，桌面办公智能体完成了第一轮普及，办公提效的价值已经成为行业共识。但当 AI 进一步走向企业核心业务，搭出一个智能体不难，难的是让它真正跑进业务流程，适配复杂的系统、权限与规则，持续产出可量化的经营价值。 在腾讯云副总裁吴永坚看来，未来企业级智能体的核心赛道，对话式的桌面办公 Agent 和服务经营的 Service Agent 会是两个长期并行的赛道。大模型提供了理解与推理能力，但想让 AI 真正参与业务经营，还需要一套能够打通系统、管好权限、支撑长期稳定运行的企业级平台。

items.description: 据路透社报道，美国民主党在国会中期选举中大胜，引发投资者对 AI 监管加强、数据中心建设放缓的担忧。 当地时间周四，美国科技股遭遇大规模抛售， 华尔街股票市值单日蒸发约 3.2 万亿美元（约合人民币 22.7 万亿元） 。纳斯达克综合指数暴跌 5.52%，创下自 2025 年 4 月以来最大单日跌幅，较 10 月初创下的历史高点累计下跌近 12%，进入技术性回调区间。

items.title: 世界互联网大会领先科技奖背后，Qoder 凭什么拿下中国 AI 编程市场第一
items.description: 2026 年 11 月，每年乌镇世界互联网大会期间举办的领先科技奖，已经走到第十年。 作为面向全球征集互联网领域领先成果的国际性科技奖项，领先科技奖每年会选出涵盖基础研究、关键技术与工程研发约 15 至 20 项获奖项目。一定程度上，它的评选也预示了未来几年潮水的走向。

items.title: 一个人用得好 AI，为什么一家公司却用不好？
items.description: 写方案、写代码、做分析报告，过去可能需要员工花费几天才能完成的任务，如今 Agent 往往能在较短时间里交出不错的结果。 但在企业里，完成一份方案，可能只是一项工作的开始。比如，Agent 可以很快制定一份员工考核方案。但要用它真正完成一次考核，还需要获取员工的考勤、业绩等数据，处理特殊情况，并经过业务负责人和 HR 的确认，才能最终确定绩效。

items.title: Apple 智能国行上线，苹果大涨超 6% 重返美股市值第一；英伟达显卡订单排长队，中国客户预计只能拿到 1%；字节限制员工使用个人 AI｜极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 4 日，Apple 智能伴随 iOS 27.3 的 Developer Beta 向中国大陆用户开放测试，并计划于 12 月随 iOS 27.3 正式版推出。与此同时，苹果也确认与阿里巴巴达成合作，将千问接入 Siri、写作工具及视觉智能，让中国用户能够通过系统直接调用国内大模型的能力。 不过，这一次上线的并不是完整版 Apple 智能。首批功能主要包括实时翻译、写作工具、视觉智能、照片消除、智绘表情、通知摘要等，而苹果此前展示的新一代 Siri AI，以及 WWDC26 公布的部分下一代 AI 能力，仍然不在此次更新范围内。

items.title: 国行版苹果 AI 开始测试；ChatGPT 搜索量已达到谷歌 20%；Seedance 被曝五成收入来自海外｜极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 4 日，苹果向开发者推送 iOS 27.3 首个 Beta 版，国行 iPhone 用户开始测试首批 Apple 智能功能，包括实时翻译、照片消除、写作工具和通知摘要等。国行 Apple 智能与阿里巴巴达成合作，在部分体验中接入千问。国内用户可直接在 Siri、写作工具和视觉智能中调用千问，覆盖文本与图像理解相关能力。 这次开放的是开发者测试版，正式版计划于 12 月推出。首批支持 iPhone 15 Pro 系列、iPhone 16 及后续机型，以及 iPhone Air 和 iPhone Duo；WWDC 2026 发布的新版 Siri AI 暂未包含在内。（来源：快科技）

items.title: AI接手运营后，速卖通潜力市场双11成交大涨超50%
items.description: 今年海外双11，中国跨境商家的订单出现在不少意想不到的“冷门”市场。 记者从阿里旗下跨境电商平台速卖通AliExpress获悉，双11大促前7日，速卖通主力市场之外的潜力国家市场日均成交同比大涨超50%。借助AI智能托管，商家们把生意做到了更多平时顾不上经营的市场。 聚光灯之外的消费者“剁手”有多积极？速卖通数据显示，“企鹅比人多”的福克兰群岛，参与大促的买家平均每人下了5.5单。地方不大，购物热情可不小； 北极圈里的斯瓦尔巴群岛，11月太阳已经“下班”，消费者们却没闲着。今年双11，斯瓦尔巴首次开单，买得最多的是玩具手办； 世界杯一战成名的“非洲黑马”佛得角，足球场上让人刮目相看，购物清单却相当务实：在速卖通上买得最多的是汽车及零配件、美容健康类商品； 全球最热的国家之一马里、和天寒地冻的挪威，对双11的热情同样高涨，GMV都实现翻倍…… “冷门”市场的订单，正汇成新的增长极。此次海外双11，速卖通南美、欧洲、东南亚、非洲四大区域的潜力国家全面增长，哥伦比亚、秘鲁、瑞士、挪威等市场表现活跃。 过去，商家知道速卖通可以“一店卖全球”，但真要接住这些订单，还得搞定不同的语言、物流、定价和大促规则。多招几个人，还是先放一放？不少商家选择了后者。 今年，速卖通上线潜力国家地区智能经营Agent，把这些琐事交给AI。商家一键启用，系统就能自动优化商品详情页、报名活动、匹配物流线路，还能提供智能客服服务，让商家在潜力市场实现自动出单。双11期间，这类接受AI运营托管的商家，日均成交同比增长近70%。 AI不仅帮助商家减负提效，也帮助商家精准推送流量，实现更快出单。平台通过算法识别托管商品的销售潜力，对有增长机会的商品提供更有针对性的流量补贴和投放支持。 这些“意料之外”的增长背后，是速卖通在潜力国家市场持续补齐物流、支付和本地化服务。据速卖通潜力市场负责人介绍，目前Choice服务已覆盖绝大多数潜力市场，让当地消费者也能享受相应的配送时效和服务保障。 此外，速卖通还在越南、挪威、坦桑尼亚、塞尔维亚等国家市场提供了32种本地化语言服务，用当地消费者熟悉的语言提升下单意愿；并接入十多个本地钱包，支付更便捷。未来，平台还将推进更多国家的本币支付，让消费者填写地址、完成付款更顺畅。 从主力市场到更多潜力国家，速卖通正通过AI能力和国别化精细运营，降低商家拓展新市场的成本，让更多中国商品获得海外订单。 在今年速卖通双11启动会上，速卖通总裁惊石表示：品牌化、本地化、AI化是速卖通今年的核心方向。双11开卖首日，速卖通品牌商品成交同比大涨200%，品牌成交的占比首次达到50%以上，涌现出一批新的百万美金品牌；海外官方仓订单环比大涨9倍，欧盟本地成交占比已突破60%。

items.title: 独家丨清华系团队创业做 AI 眼镜，拿下传统眼镜厂商种子轮
items.description: 雷峰网·鲸犀独家获悉， 智能眼镜初创公司深圳市清目数字科技有限公司 （下文简称清目数字 ） 已完成种子轮融资，投资方为南京视客 ，天使轮融资正在推进中。 清目数字首款产品定位职场办公场景， 采用双目双波导显示、多麦克风阵列、双喇叭导音方案，无摄像头，整机 31.7 克 。目前硬件方案已定型并完成工程样机，进入 EVT 阶段，首版电路板点亮，App 闭环 Demo 跑通。

items.title: 灵光接入什么值得买，AI助理开始帮用户“盯好价”
items.description: 从商品推荐到价格追踪，个人AI助理进一步深入日常消费场景。 11月10日消息，蚂蚁集团旗下个人AI助理灵光接入消费内容平台「什么值得买」，将商品信息、消费决策支持等服务进一步纳入灵光。 此次接入是灵光持续扩展开放服务生态的又一动作。此前，灵光已陆续接入支付宝、钉钉、飞书、米家、微信读书、哈啰打车等40个连接器服务，能力覆盖工作、出行、家庭管理和日常生活等多个场景。 「什么值得买」长期积累了商品信息、消费内容和优惠信息等资源。对于灵光而言，接入专业消费信息服务，有助于提升AI在具体消费场景中的信息获取和服务能力；对于什么值得买而言，个人AI助理也提供了一个新的用户需求入口。此次连接「什么值得买」后，灵光将更加精准的实现持续关注商品价格变化，管理好用户“买什么、什么时候买更划算”这类日常事务。 对于消费者而言，购物的一大难题并不是下单，而是如何在海量商品、复杂促销和不断变化的价格中作出判断。以购买一台扫地机器人为例： 过去，用户通常需要在多个平台之间比较型号、配置、价格和促销活动。如果暂时不买，还需要反复查看商品是否降价、优惠如何叠加，费时费力。 现在，用户在灵光App输入“双11准备买一个扫地机器人，帮我看看哪款扫地机器人更值得买？”借助与什么值得买的服务连接，灵光会自主完成扫地机器人的优劣对比和好价监控，若用户暂时不买，灵光则会持续监控扫地机器人的价格优惠，并及时推送给用户。 这种变化也意味着，AI在消费场景中的作用正从一次性的信息查询，向持续性的消费决策辅助延伸。 对于个人AI助理而言，模型能力决定了它能否理解用户需求，而外部服务生态则决定了它能否真正参与用户生活。随着专业消费服务接入，个人AI助理的竞争正在从单纯的模型交互能力，延伸到真实服务供给和跨平台事务管理能力。用户未来可能不再需要为每一个消费需求反复打开不同App，而是将需求交给AI，由AI持续跟进，并在合适的时间提供决策支持。 据了解，10月27日，蚂蚁集团推出灵光2.0，将产品定位升级为“能管事的个人AI助理”。与传统问答式AI不同，灵光2.0能够在获得用户授权后，持续跟进相关事务，并在重要节点主动提醒用户。 雷峰网 雷峰网

items.title: 四维图新创想大会 | 以数据与算力为基，SEEWAY.AI驶向新一站
items.description: 11月6日，四维图新在上海举办2026 EVOLUTION创想大会。CEO 程鹏全面解读穿越 “极点” 的破局方向，以数据与算力为基，答行业焦点之问，并正式公布向移动智能体领域拓展的战略布局。 "过去十年，中国新能源赢在电池；未来十年，中国汽车要赢在数据。"程鹏的判断直指行业下一个核心战场——数据已成为汽车智能化的"第二战场"，而用好数据的前提，是合规。

items.title: Fable 5.2 “撞车”蚂蚁灵波触觉模型，CEO 朱兴：两类模型协同将加速具身产业成熟
items.description: 11 月 10 日，Claude Fable 5.2 发布同日，蚂蚁灵波科技开源触觉基础模型 LingBot-Touch。一款面向数字世界的通用大模型，一款面向物理操作闭环的具身基础模型，同一天走进公众视野。 这两条技术路线的关系，正是当下具身智能行业讨论的焦点。在蚂蚁灵波看来，通用大模型与具身基础模型更接近 1+1＞2 的协同关系：前者增强对任务和环境的理解与推理，后者补齐物理感知与闭环操作能力，两者齐头并进，才能共同加速具身产业成熟。 此次开源的 LingBot-Touch 基于近 5000 小时真实触觉数据预训练，覆盖磁触觉、视触觉和压阻式三类主流传感原理，可将不同信号转化为同一套触觉表征，供不同灵巧手和动作模型使用，让机器人在“看得清楚、想得明白”的同时，进一步补齐精细操作所需的触觉感知。 此前，蚂蚁灵波通用大脑已覆盖高精度空间感知、高动态环境交互和可泛化灵巧操作，此次 LingBot-Touch 已接入 LingBot-VLA，将感知能力延伸到“指尖”，让机器人“摸得更灵敏”，具身原生通用大脑的手眼协同能力再上台阶。 26 项真机测试，任务成功率提高 14 至 26 个百分点 随着通用大模型持续进步，机器人理解复杂任务、推理操作步骤的能力正在增强。但在真实物理世界中，机器人每执行一步动作，都要感知物体和环境的变化，再修正下一步动作。许多精细操作里，机器人能看清物体在哪里，也能把手伸到正确位置，却未必能顺利完成任务——手指碰到物体之后，受力是否合适、物体是否滑移，仅靠视觉难以判断，需要触觉来补位。 以灵巧手拧瓶盖为例，深度信息可以帮助手指对准瓶盖；开始转动后，瓶盖可能已经松动，也可能指腹正沿着盖壁打滑。这两种情况在画面中相似，却需要不同的动作调整。指尖的接触位置、受力大小及其变化，往往被手指和物体遮挡，视觉难以获得，却正是动作模型的重要判断依据。 为验证触觉表征对真实操作的帮助，蚂蚁灵波在 Sharpa Wave 和 XHand1 两款灵巧手上进行了 26 项真机测试，涵盖翻书页、拧瓶盖、辨识麻将牌等精细操作。接入 LingBot-Touch 后，LingBot-VLA、π0.5、Diffusion Policy 和 T-Rex 四种动作模型的平均任务成功率较无触觉时提高约 14 至 26 个百分点。以 T-Rex 控制 Sharpa Wave 拧瓶盖为例，不使用触觉时任务成功率为 56.25%，直接输入传感器原始信号为 62.5%，接入 LingBot-Touch 触觉表征后成功率达到 90%。 （图说：接入 LingBot-Touch 后，四种动作模型在两款灵巧手上的真机任务成功率均达到各自最高水平） 统一触觉表征，让“手感”跨硬件、跨模型、跨任务复用 给机器人装上触觉传感器，并不等于它就能用好触觉。目前商用触觉传感器整体仍处于较早的发展阶段，视触觉、磁触觉、压阻式等主流路线各有所长、也各有局限，面向不同成本和使用场景，多种技术路线可能长期并存。更棘手的是，这些传感器采集的数据很难直接通用：同样一次接触，在不同传感原理和触点布局下会形成不同的原始信号，模型一旦只学会解读其中一种，更换传感器或灵巧手后，已有的数据和触觉经验就可能难以复用，需要重新采集、训练和适配。 因此，触觉走向规模化落地的关键，是让触觉理解摆脱对特定传感器物理信号的依赖，使不同来源的数据能够共同用于训练，让积累的触觉能力可以跨传感器、跨灵巧手、跨模型和跨任务复用。 为此，LingBot-Touch 按传感原理分别设置编码入口，先处理不同的原始信号，再将不同布局的触点映射到统一的指尖坐标空间，由共享模型学习接触位置、受力及其随时间的变化，输出统一的触觉 Token。由此，人戴触觉手套和遥操作灵巧手采集的数据可以共同用于训练，不同动作模型也可以直接调用训练好的模型提取接触特征，这一架构还为未来接入新型触觉传感器留出了扩展空间。 （图说：LingBot-Touch 将磁触觉、视触觉、压阻式触觉信号编码为统一的触觉 Token，供不同动作模型使用） 在 XHand1 上，团队进一步验证了触觉能力的跨硬件复用：XHand1 采用的磁触觉传感器型号并不在预训练数据中，模型学到的磁触觉经验全部来自人戴手套采集的数据。换到这只灵巧手后，团队保持…

items.title: 41年爱妻人设崩塌！黄仁勋一夜损失3万亿，或被英伟达免职；曝一汽大众取消两年「年终奖」，有人称合计约20万；豆包新图像模型价格下降
items.description: 11月10日消息，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋近期爆出的私人婚外情丑闻，在资本市场引发了剧烈连锁反应，公司美股股价盘中一度下跌8.8%。按丑闻曝出前英伟达约4.5万亿美元的总市值计算，当天盘中最大市值缩水额度接近3960亿美元（约2.81万亿人民币），直接创下了全球上市公司因高管个人丑闻引发的最大单日市值损失纪录。在这次股价大幅波动里，黄仁勋本人直接持有的英伟达股份账面价值，也一度缩水约143亿美元，换算成人民币约为1015亿元。 此前报道，英伟达CEO黄仁勋11月8日承认出轨，英伟达已对其展开调查。美国投资机构Yorkville Ives合伙人兼高级董事总经理丹·艾夫斯表示：“显然，根据董事会的调查结果，黄仁勋可能被免去首席执行官职务。”作为英伟达联合创始人，黄仁勋以亲力亲为、不知疲倦的管理风格著称。英伟达至今尚未公布明确的接班计划，黄仁勋也没有明显指定接班人。

items.title: 千问办公2.0，补上了办公Agent最关键的「短板」
items.description: “过去几个月，各家都在拼命证明AI越来越能干活。但说实话，一个人能干活，不代表一群人就能协作。” 一位长期关注AI办公的业内人士，试用完市面上主流的AI办公产品后发现，有些“麻烦”还是绕不开，最典型的就是有些活儿还得靠人工来回“倒腾”。

items.title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
items.description: The governance experts we talked to say nobody has seen anything like what's unfolding right now.

items.title: OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder
items.description: OpenAI has not yet said what its plans are for the future of travel. But Sonder founder Francis Davidson is a well-known figure in the travel industry.

items.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
items.description: New York is preparing to enforce its sweeping AI safety law, requiring major developers like OpenAI and Anthropic to register, disclose safety practices, and report critical incidents or face fines.

items.title: All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO
items.description: Each of the seven co-founders plans to sell exactly the same number of shares in the IPO, which would bring each of them about $250 million in cash at the midpoint of the price range while leaving the group in control of the company.

items.title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
items.description: The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”

items.title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
items.description: PSI used an unreleased Anthropic model to answer a fundamental question about quantum computing that scientists have pursued for nearly two decades.

items.title: OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
items.description: OpenAI is looking to make ChatGPT a more robust consumer discovery engine, and a host of new features seek to empower businesses to help it do that.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks
items.description: As participants talk, Claude can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year's figures.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy: a timeline
items.description: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.

items.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
items.description: Google's new tensor processing units (TPUs) broaden its chip portfolio to more use cases: confidential model training and more memory capacity.

items.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
items.description: Users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation on their Apple Watch.

items.title: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly
items.description: Adobe is taking on Figma with a new prototype builder tool in Firefly.

items.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
items.description: The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis.

items.title: After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era
items.description: Kora is set to launch as a free-to-use alternative to Windows, targeting users who rely heavily on AI models and agents.

items.title: Spotify’s AI DJ gets new voices, personalities, and an option for less chatter
items.description: Spotify Premium users can now customize their AI DJ with new voices with different personalities, or turn off the commentary between songs.

items.title: Ring, known for its doorbell cameras, launches a home security drone and an enterprise security robot
items.description: Amazon-owned Ring is pushing into robotics with the launch of a home security drone and a rolling robot designed to patrol and protect businesses.

items.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns
items.description: Hugging Face executive Irene Solaiman warns that growing cyberattacks on open AI platforms could force tighter security restrictions, threatening the accessibility that makes open source communities valuable to developers worldwide.

items.title: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages
items.description: Otter AI just added support for 27 languages and revealed an upcoming feature that can follow along if speakers switch between languages.

items.title: Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans
items.description: The AI company is expected to set its valuation range this week, the Wall Street Journal reported.

items.title: Jensen Huang reportedly engaged a PR firm with a history of handling high-profile sex scandals a year ago
items.description: The PR firm was enlisted shortly after an October 2025 New York Times report described Alice Huang's business dealings with Jensen Huang, Wired reported.

items.title: OpenAI turns ChatGPT into a business directory with AI agents that handle customer questions
items.description: OpenAI is opening up ChatGPT as a business platform: through a new Business Hub, companies can claim their profile, add product data, and track how users interact with them. "Business Agents" let eligible US e-commerce providers talk to customers directly inside ChatGPT.

items.title: Anthropic turns Claude into a full workspace with Plugins, spreadsheets, whiteboards, and soon Meeting notes
items.description: Anthropic is expanding Claude with Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors, letting partners like Adobe and Atlassian embed their apps directly inside Claude. Anthropic says Claude Meetings, which can join calls and take notes, is coming soon. Step by step, Anthropic is turning Claude into a central work platform for teams that brings many other apps together in one place.

items.title: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot
items.description: Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to teach robots new tasks without laborious teleoperation. Instead, the system transfers human hand movements from videos to robotic arms, trained on about 400,000 hours of video footage. Success rates still vary widely, though, ranging from 10 to 80 percent depending on the task.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon arrives just in time to feel like yesterday's news in the fastest model cycle yet
items.description: Google is making Gemini 4 Carbon generally available after a two-week testing phase. The model ranks first in several benchmarks, in some cases ahead of Anthropic's new Fable 5.2, at less than half the per-task cost. Google is also previewing coordinated agent teams through the "/swarm" feature, which split up complex tasks in real time.

items.title: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96 percent sorting metal parts in a Mercedes-Benz assembly pilot
items.description: Google Deepmind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new control model for robots, and tested it with Apptronik on active Mercedes-Benz production lines in Hungary and Germany. The humanoid robot Apollo 2 sorted metal parts there with a reported success rate of 96 percent.

items.title: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 completes 41 percent of real freelance jobs, up from 2.5 percent a year ago
items.description: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 completes 41.3 percent of real freelance jobs at professional quality on the Remote Labor Index, more than double the next-best systems Opus 5.5 and GPT 6 Astra. A year ago the top score was 2.5 percent. Areas like product design and animation remain a weak spot.

items.title: Eight countries and top AI labs agree to shutdown mechanisms in new Paris declaration
items.description: Eight countries along with representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Mistral AI have signed the "Paris Call for AI Safety and Security" at Emmanuel Macron's initiative. The companies commit to shutdown mechanisms, independent audits, and disclosing known risks, but the agreement lacks binding sanctions or deadlines.

items.title: Anthropic kicks off IPO roadshow, offering shares at $70 to $78 and targeting a trillion-dollar valuation
items.description: Anthropic is kicking off its IPO roadshow, targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion. Beyond the public offering of up to $64.4 billion, the company is securing $26 billion through a private placement with Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, and other major tech firms as anchor investors. The IPO comes at a time when investors are growing increasingly skeptical of AI investments.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 cement Anthropic's AI lead just before its IPO
items.description: Anthropic is releasing Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, its most powerful models to date, in two versions: one freely available and one reserved for verified organizations. The models solve open physics problems, show stronger cybersecurity capabilities, design functioning operating systems, and write more than 90 percent of the changes merged into Anthropic's core code, according to the company. Anthropic says it has deliberately curbed any capabilities that would let the AI accelerate its own development.

items.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small AI model built for the repetitive work agents actually do
items.description: Meta is introducing Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model, optimized for repetitive agent tasks such as tool calls, routing, and data extraction. According to Meta, it delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna. But it falls short when it comes to actual programming tasks.

items.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
items.description: As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world's most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes […]

items.title: ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’
items.description: ChatGPT is going to let you chat with verified "Business Agents" that represent a brand to help you with things like comparison shopping. The feature, available first to "eligible" e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, is launching as part of a suite of business-focused features in ChatGPT being announced today in beta. You […]

items.title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
items.description: Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in "any capacity." Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it "sparingly" used AI in the "final stretch" of the game's development to "help work through difficult […]

items.title: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
items.description: For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs - like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta - to copy its strategies. Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint […]

items.title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
items.description: eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing on the platform - the latest speed bump in the AI agent race. A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he's had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a […]

items.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
items.description: Google is rolling out its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public after releasing it to a select group of "cybersecurity defenders" two weeks ago. Google claims Carbon is its "strongest model" yet, and capable of competing with the very best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI. Google says Gemini 4 Carbon "pushes […]

items.title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
items.description: Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the The New York Times. The Wall Street Journal […]

items.title: Adobe is going all in on agentic AI
items.description: Adobe is committing itself to the notion that chatbots and AI agents could be your next design assistant, or even automate creative workflows and repetitive tasks on your behalf. Some of the tools and features announced today at Adobe's Max conference in Miami, Florida, include allowing your preferred third-party AI agents to access and change […]

items.title: Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere are making it easier to remove things
items.description: Adobe is expanding its Creative Cloud apps and Firefly AI platform with new capabilities that aim to make design and editing projects faster and less complicated. Some of the announcements from Adobe's Max event today include features for automatically removing objects, blemishes, and other unwanted distractions in Premiere, Photoshop, and Lightroom, alongside new generative AI […]

items.title: Hands-on with Ring’s new AI drone camera for your home
items.description: Ring is finally shipping a flying indoor drone camera. For real this time. The Ring Drone Cam will arrive on January 27th, 2027, for $249.99, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said at a launch event in New York City this week. If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced […]

items.title: Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark: testing knowledge work capabilities with complex visual files
items.description: We’ve partnered with Google DeepMind to launch their Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) evaluation, a new benchmark for agentic knowledge work over complex visual files

items.title: Endpoint Accuracy Index v1.1: Tighter long context intervals and expanded model coverage
items.description: We are launching the Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index v1.1, a minor version upgrade alongside new coverage for GLM-5.3 Flash and Muse Spark Open.

items.title: Meta's Muse Ember is the cheapest model scoring 36 on the Intelligence Index
items.description: Meta's newest model Muse Ember scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at a third of the Cost per Task

items.title: Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2
items.description: Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2: a new proprietary evaluation, updated benchmarks, and a headline metric that rewards model calibration

items.title: VIALS-AA: different paths to scientific image reasoning
items.description: Independent VIALS-AA results, interactive agent traces, and an analysis of how models inspect scientific images.

items.title: Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Small: the highest scoring open weights model outside of China pending weights release
items.description: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index - their plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings

items.title: Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B scoring 20 on the Intelligence Index
items.description: Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B, an open weights model matching Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with stronger terminal use but weaker knowledge

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
items.description: Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

items.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion orchestrates Anthropic and OpenAI models to balance performance and cost
items.description: itHub has released Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot, which orchestrates between Anthropic and OpenAI models. It scores 2 points below Opus 5.5 in Claude Code at half the Cost per Task in the Coding Agent Index

items.title: Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
items.description: Index v5 features 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra pushes the cost efficiency frontier
items.description: OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra, pushing the cost efficiency frontier. It is the first Terra-class model since GPT-5.6, and is more intelligent for less than a third of the cost

items.title: Code2Video-AA: how well do AI models design videos in code?
items.description: Artificial Analysis' implementation of HeyGen's Code2Video Bench, evaluating how well models create short product and brand videos from 114 design briefs using HyperFrames HTML.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Intelligence Index and will lead open weights models
items.description: Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and will lead open weights models

items.title: HealthBench and HealthBench Professional: Evaluating models in realistic health conversations
items.description: We’re launching leaderboards for HealthBench and HealthBench Professional, two benchmarks evaluating how AI models respond in realistic health conversations

items.title: Announcing AA-PersonalityBench: measuring how AI models communicate
items.description: AA-PersonalityBench measures the personality and communication style of AI models. A panel of LLM judges compares answers pairwise on 30 personality traits, which roll up into 8 personality indexes, alongside 21 communication characteristics measured directly from every response.

items.title: Reflection has released Beam, their first model launch
items.description: Reflection’s first model, Beam, scores 30 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it #2 among US open weights models

items.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B A9B
items.description: Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now the leading US open weight model, scoring 26 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

items.title: First AA-AgentPerf results for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72
items.description: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 serves up to ~5.7x the total throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 on AA-AgentPerf, with first results on DeepSeek V4 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3.

items.title: First AA-AgentPerf-Local results for an NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X laptop
items.description: An NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X laptop completes our local agent workload on Qwen3.8 27B in 18.7 minutes.

items.title: Welcome to the era of embodied AI: Introducing AA-Robotics v0.1
items.description: We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

items.title: Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0
items.description: The Artificial Analysis Decision Index benchmarks decision models, a new category of models that answer structured decisions in a single call with a probability for each option. Version 1.0 combines four evaluations across classification, tool calling, knowledge, hallucination, and reasoning.

items.title: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: a material jump in intelligence over previous Meta models
items.description: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, achieving Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 scores of 52 and 56 at max reasoning effort - each a material gain over Muse Spark 1.3 (max) at 48, with a release gap of only 6 weeks

items.title: Announcing AA-3D: a benchmark for AI models building interactive 3D experiences
items.description: AA-3D is a new benchmark of how well AI models build interactive 3D experiences. Each model turns a written brief into a working three.js scene in an offline sandbox, and our recruited panel compares the scenes in blind pairwise votes.

items.title: Announcing FrontierCode on Artificial Analysis: can AI models write code maintainers would merge?
items.description: Cognition's FrontierCode 1.1 tests whether AI models make code changes that maintainers of real open source repositories would merge. Leading models still fail more than 40% of the time.

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.description: On the first day of AIE Code Summit, OpenAI showed how developers can steer Codex by voice, hand off work to the cloud, and make use of dots.

items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.description: Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send.

items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.description: NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek.

items.title: [AINews] Fable 5.2 retakes World #1 LLM spot as $ANT IPO roadshow begins
items.description: November 9, 2026 — Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive on Anthropic’s IPO roadshow day. How much thinking is worth paying for?

items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team

items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.description: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: ai , prompt-engineering , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.description: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

items.title: Quoting Nilay Patel
items.description: The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs. You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history. It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked. The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop. The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products . Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better. — Nilay Patel , The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election Tags: ai , generative-ai , slop , nilay-patel , ai-ethics

items.description: My comment on AI is destroying my CS degree — Hacker News. I don't envy educators right now. AI clearly means you need to change how you teach and evaluate students. items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.description: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

items.title: llm 0.37
items.description: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! Tags: open-source , projects , ai , annotated-release-notes , generative-ai , llms , embeddings , llm

items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.description: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

items.title: dbreunig/nesformer
items.description: dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. Followed by: I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.description: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , gpt , ted-sanders

items.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
items.description: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. Tags: github , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , disclosures , agentic-engineering

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.description: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds: Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier…

items.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
items.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.description: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

items.title: Why We Think
items.description: Special thanks to John Schulman for a lot of super valuable feedback and direct edits on this post. Test time compute ( Graves et al. 2016 , Ling, et al. 2017 , Cobbe et al. 2021 ) and Chain-of-thought (CoT) ( Wei et al. 2022 , Nye et al. 2021 ), have led to significant improvements in model performance, while raising many research questions. This post aims to review recent developments in how to effectively use test-time compute (i.e. “thinking time”) and why it helps.

items.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
items.description: Reward hacking occurs when a reinforcement learning (RL) agent exploits flaws or ambiguities in the reward function to achieve high rewards, without genuinely learning or completing the intended task. Reward hacking exists because RL environments are often imperfect, and it is fundamentally challenging to accurately specify a reward function. With the rise of language models generalizing to a broad spectrum of tasks and RLHF becomes a de facto method for alignment training, reward hacking in RL training of language models has become a critical practical challenge. Instances where the model learns to modify unit tests to pass coding tasks, or where responses contain biases that mimic a user’s preference, are pretty concerning and are likely one of the major blockers for real-world deployment of more autonomous use cases of AI models.

items.title: Extrinsic Hallucinations in LLMs
items.description: Hallucination in large language models usually refers to the model generating unfaithful, fabricated, inconsistent, or nonsensical content. As a term, hallucination has been somewhat generalized to cases when the model makes mistakes. Here, I would like to narrow down the problem of hallucination to cases where the model output is fabricated and not grounded by either the provided context or world knowledge. There are two types of hallucination: In-context hallucination: The model output should be consistent with the source content in context. Extrinsic hallucination: The model output should be grounded by the pre-training dataset. However, given the size of the pre-training dataset, it is too expensive to retrieve and identify conflicts per generation. If we consider the pre-training data corpus as a proxy for world knowledge, we essentially try to ensure the model output is factual and verifiable by external world knowledge. Equally importantly, when the model does not know about a fact, it should say so. This post focuses on extrinsic hallucination. To avoid hallucination, LLMs need to be (1) factual and (2) acknowledge not knowing the answer when applicable.

items.title: Diffusion Models for Video Generation
items.description: Diffusion models have demonstrated strong results on image synthesis in past years. Now the research community has started working on a harder task—using it for video generation. The task itself is a superset of the image case, since an image is a video of 1 frame, and it is much more challenging because: It has extra requirements on temporal consistency across frames in time, which naturally demands more world knowledge to be encoded into the model. In comparison to text or images, it is more difficult to collect large amounts of high-quality, high-dimensional video data, let along text-video pairs. 🥑 Required Pre-read: Please make sure you have read the previous blog on “What are Diffusion Models?” for image generation before continue here.

items.title: Thinking about High-Quality Human Data
items.description: [Special thank you to Ian Kivlichan for many useful pointers (E.g. the 100+ year old Nature paper “Vox populi”) and nice feedback. 🙏 ] High-quality data is the fuel for modern data deep learning model training. Most of the task-specific labeled data comes from human annotation, such as classification task or RLHF labeling (which can be constructed as classification format) for LLM alignment training. Lots of ML techniques in the post can help with data quality, but fundamentally human data collection involves attention to details and careful execution. The community knows the value of high quality data, but somehow we have this subtle impression that “Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work” ( Sambasivan et al. 2021 ).

items.title: Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
items.description: The use of large language models in the real world has strongly accelerated by the launch of ChatGPT. We (including my team at OpenAI, shoutout to them) have invested a lot of effort to build default safe behavior into the model during the alignment process (e.g. via RLHF ). However, adversarial attacks or jailbreak prompts could potentially trigger the model to output something undesired. A large body of ground work on adversarial attacks is on images, and differently it operates in the continuous, high-dimensional space. Attacks for discrete data like text have been considered to be a lot more challenging, due to lack of direct gradient signals. My past post on Controllable Text Generation is quite relevant to this topic, as attacking LLMs is essentially to control the model to output a certain type of (unsafe) content.

items.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
items.description: Building agents with LLM (large language model) as its core controller is a cool concept. Several proof-of-concepts demos, such as AutoGPT , GPT-Engineer and BabyAGI , serve as inspiring examples. The potentiality of LLM extends beyond generating well-written copies, stories, essays and programs; it can be framed as a powerful general problem solver. Agent System Overview In a LLM-powered autonomous agent system, LLM functions as the agent’s brain, complemented by several key components: Planning Subgoal and decomposition: The agent breaks down large tasks into smaller, manageable subgoals, enabling efficient handling of complex tasks. Reflection and refinement: The agent can do self-criticism and self-reflection over past actions, learn from mistakes and refine them for future steps, thereby improving the quality of final results. Memory Short-term memory: I would consider all the in-context learning (See Prompt Engineering ) as utilizing short-term memory of the model to learn. Long-term memory: This provides the agent with the capability to retain and recall (infinite) information over extended periods, often by leveraging an external vector store and fast retrieval. Tool use The agent learns to call external APIs for extra information that is missing from the model weights (often hard to change after pre-training), including current information, code execution capability, access to proprietary information sources and more. Overview of a LLM-powered autonomous agent system. Component One: Planning A complicated task usually involves many steps. An agent needs to know what they are and plan ahead.

items.title: Prompt Engineering
items.description: Prompt Engineering , also known as In-Context Prompting , refers to methods for how to communicate with LLM to steer its behavior for desired outcomes without updating the model weights. It is an empirical science and the effect of prompt engineering methods can vary a lot among models, thus requiring heavy experimentation and heuristics. This post only focuses on prompt engineering for autoregressive language models, so nothing with Cloze tests, image generation or multimodality models. At its core, the goal of prompt engineering is about alignment and model steerability. Check my previous post on controllable text generation.

items.title: The Transformer Family Version 2.0
items.description: Many new Transformer architecture improvements have been proposed since my last post on “The Transformer Family” about three years ago. Here I did a big refactoring and enrichment of that 2020 post — restructure the hierarchy of sections and improve many sections with more recent papers. Version 2.0 is a superset of the old version, about twice the length. The Transformer (which will be referred to as “vanilla Transformer” to distinguish it from other enhanced versions; Vaswani, et al., 2017 ) model has an encoder-decoder architecture, as commonly used in many NMT models. Later simplified Transformer was shown to achieve great performance in language modeling tasks, like in encoder-only BERT or decoder-only GPT .

They are powerful but very expensive to train and use. The extremely high inference cost, in both time and memory, is a big bottleneck for adopting a powerful transformer for solving real-world tasks at scale. Why is it hard to run inference for large transformer models? Besides the increasing size of SoTA models, there are two main factors contributing to the inference challenge ( Pope et al. 2022 ):

items.title: Some Math behind Neural Tangent Kernel
items.description: Neural networks are well known to be over-parameterized and can often easily fit data with near-zero training loss with decent generalization performance on test dataset. Although all these parameters are initialized at random, the optimization process can consistently lead to similarly good outcomes. And this is true even when the number of model parameters exceeds the number of training data points. Neural tangent kernel (NTK) ( Jacot et al. 2018 ) is a kernel to explain the evolution of neural networks during training via gradient descent. It leads to great insights into why neural networks with enough width can consistently converge to a global minimum when trained to minimize an empirical loss. In the post, we will do a deep dive into the motivation and definition of NTK, as well as the proof of a deterministic convergence at different initializations of neural networks with infinite width by characterizing NTK in such a setting.

items.title: Generalized Visual Language Models
items.description: Processing images to generate text, such as image captioning and visual question-answering, has been studied for years. Traditionally such systems rely on an object detection network as a vision encoder to capture visual features and then produce text via a text decoder. Given a large amount of existing literature, in this post, I would like to only focus on one approach for solving vision language tasks, which is to extend pre-trained generalized language models to be capable of consuming visual signals .

items.title: Learning with not Enough Data Part 3: Data Generation
items.description: Here comes the Part 3 on learning with not enough data (Previous: Part 1 and Part 2 ). Let’s consider two approaches for generating synthetic data for training. Augmented data . Given a set of existing training samples, we can apply a variety of augmentation, distortion and transformation to derive new data points without losing the key attributes. We have covered a bunch of augmentation methods on text and images in a previous post on contrastive learning. For the sake of post completeness, I duplicate the section on data augmentation here with some edits. New data . Given few or even no data points, we can rely on powerful pretrained models to generate a number of new data points. This is especially true in recent years given the fast progress in large pretrained language models (LM) . Few shot prompting is shown to be effective for LM to learn within context without extra training. Data Augmentation The goal of data augmentation is to modify the input format (e.g. text wording, visual appearance) while the semantic meaning stays unchanged.

items.description: The goal of contrastive representation learning is to learn such an embedding space in which similar sample pairs stay close to each other while dissimilar ones are far apart. Contrastive learning can be applied to both supervised and unsupervised settings. When working with unsupervised data, contrastive learning is one of the most powerful approaches in self-supervised learning .

items.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
items.description: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case.

items.title: Claude’s new auto eval tool
items.description: Anthropic released new eval tooling for Claude Code . Their claude-api plugin now includes a new build_eval and hill-climb command that helps you build evals, check the graders, and improve your application against them. I usually don’t review eval tools because software changes so often that reviews have a short shelf life. But a first-party tool from Anthropic is likely to influence how people approach evals, so I wanted to try it and share what I found.

items.title: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know
items.description: This document curates the most common questions Shreya and I received while teaching 5,000+ engineers and PMs AI Evals. Warning: These are sharp opinions about what works in most cases. They are not universal truths. Use your judgment. Browse the questions that interest you, or choose a guide below for a curated reading path through the FAQs and related articles.

items.title: AI Product Engineering Notes
items.description: Notes from 13 sessions on evals, context, and systems. 9.5 hours of talks distilled into about 20 minutes of reading.

items.title: “It’s Hard to Eval” Is a Product Smell
items.description: For the past 3 years, AI evals have been my professional focus. 1 The most common objection I hear to evals is “our product is hard to eval”. This objection is a product smell. Artifacts that are hard for you to verify are often hard for users too. In the worst case, users have to redo the work from scratch to verify the output. More importantly, designing your product for ease of verification should come before building evals.

items.title: The Revenge of the Data Scientist
items.description: Is the heyday of the data scientist over? The Harvard Business Review once called it “The Sexiest Job of the 21st Century.” 1 In tech, data scientist roles were often among the best paid. 2 The job also demanded an unusual mix of skills: Data Scientist (n.): Person who is better at statistics than any software engineer and better at software engineering than any statistician.

items.title: Evals Skills for Coding Agents
items.description: Today, Shreya Shankar and I are publishing evals skills , a set of skills for AI product evals 1 . Eval tools often get in the way. They nudge you toward generic off-the-shelf metrics and fully automated evals before you’ve looked at your data. These skills help you avoid common mistakes we’ve seen helping 50+ companies and teaching students in our AI Evals course .

items.title: Why I Stopped Using nbdev
items.description: Programmers love to proclaim they’ve found the best tool. Paul Graham called Lisp his “ secret weapon .” DHH described Ruby as “ a magical glove that just fit my brain perfectly .” Pieter Levels ships million-dollar products with vanilla PHP and jQuery . These declarations aren’t about the languages themselves. They’re about developers finding tools that fit how they think. When the environment clicks, you move fast.

items.title: Selecting The Right AI Evals Tool
items.description: Over the past year, I’ve focused heavily on AI Evals , both in my consulting work and teaching. A question I get constantly is, “What’s the best tool for evals?”. I’ve always resisted answering directly for two reasons. First, people focus too much on tools instead of the process, thinking the tool will be an off-the-shelf solution when it rarely is. Second, the tools change so quickly that comparisons become outdated immediately. Having used many of the popular eval tools, I can genuinely say that no single one is superior in every dimension. The “best” tool depends on your team’s skillset, technical stack, and maturity.

items.title: Common pitfalls when building generative AI applications
items.description: As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience. Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

items.title: Agents
items.description: Intelligent agents are considered by many to be the ultimate goal of AI. The classic book by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (Prentice Hall, 1995), defines the field of AI research as “ the study and design of rational agents. ” The unprecedented capabilities of foundation models have opened the door to agentic applications that were previously unimaginable. These new capabilities make it finally possible to develop autonomous, intelligent agents to act as our assistants, coworkers, and coaches. They can help us create a website, gather data, plan a trip, do market research, manage a customer account, automate data entry, prepare us for interviews, interview our candidates, negotiate a deal, etc. The possibilities seem endless, and the potential economic value of these agents is enormous.

items.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
items.description: After studying how companies deploy generative AI applications, I noticed many similarities in their platforms. This post outlines the common components of a generative AI platform, what they do, and how they are implemented. I try my best to keep the architecture general, but certain applications might deviate. This is what the overall architecture looks like. This is a pretty complex system. This post will start from the simplest architecture and progressively add more components. In its simplest form, your application receives a query and sends it to the model. The model generates a response, which is returned to the user. There are no guardrails, no augmented context, and no optimization. The Model API box refers to both third-party APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) and self-hosted APIs.

items.title: Measuring personal growth
items.description: My founder friends constantly think about growth. They think about how to measure their business growth and how to get to the next order of magnitude scale. If they’re making $1M ARR today, they think about how to get to $10M ARR. If they have 1,000 users today, they think about how to get to 10,000 users. This made me wonder if/how people are measuring personal growth. I don’t want to use metrics like net worth or the number of followers, because that’s not what I live for. After talking with a lot of friends, I found three interesting metrics: rate of change, time to solve problems, and number of future options.

items.title: Predictive Human Preference: From Model Ranking to Model Routing
items.description: A challenge of building AI applications is choosing which model to use. What if we don’t have to? What if we can predict the best model for any prompt? Predictive human preference aims to predict which model users might prefer for a specific query. Human preference has emerged to be both the Northstar and a powerful tool for AI model development. Human preference guides post-training techniques including RLHF and DPO . Human preference is also used to rank AI models, as used by LMSYS’s Chatbot Arena .

items.title: Generation configurations: temperature, top-k, top-p, and test time compute
items.description: ML models are probabilistic. Imagine that you want to know what’s the best cuisine in the world. If you ask someone this question twice, a minute apart, their answers both times should be the same. If you ask a model the same question twice, its answer can change. If the model thinks that Vietnamese cuisine has a 70% chance of being the best cuisine and Italian cuisine has a 30% chance, it’ll answer “Vietnamese” 70% of the time, and “Italian” 30%. This probabilistic nature makes AI great for creative tasks. What is creativity but the ability to explore beyond the common possibilities, to think outside the box?

items.title: Multimodality and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)
items.description: For a long time, each ML model operated in one data mode – text (translation, language modeling), image (object detection, image classification), or audio (speech recognition). However, natural intelligence is not limited to just a single modality. Humans can read, talk, and see. We listen to music to relax and watch out for strange noises to detect danger. Being able to work with multimodal data is essential for us or any AI to operate in the real world.

items.title: Open challenges in LLM research
items.description: [ LinkedIn discussion , Twitter thread ] Never before in my life had I seen so many smart people working on the same goal: making LLMs better. After talking to many people working in both industry and academia, I noticed the 10 major research directions that emerged. The first two directions, hallucinations and context learning, are probably the most talked about today. I’m the most excited about numbers 3 (multimodality), 5 (new architecture), and 6 (GPU alternatives).

items.title: microgpt
items.description: This is a brief guide to my new art project microgpt , a single file of 200 lines of pure Python with no dependencies that trains and inferences a GPT. This file contains the full algorithmic content of what is needed: dataset of documents, tokenizer, autograd engine, a GPT-2-like neural network architecture, the Adam optimizer, training loop, and inference loop. Everything else is just efficiency. I cannot simplify this any further. This script is the culmination of multiple projects (micrograd, makemore, nanogpt, etc.) and a decade-long obsession to simplify LLMs to their bare essentials, and I think it is beautiful 🥹. It even breaks perfectly across 3 columns: The following is my guide on stepping an interested reader through the code.

items.title: Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now
items.description: The Yann LeCun et al. (1989) paper Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition is I believe of some historical significance because it is, to my knowledge, the earliest real-world application of a neural net trained end-to-end with backpropagation. Except for the tiny dataset (7291 16x16 grayscale images of digits) and the tiny neural network used (only 1,000 neurons), this paper reads remarkably modern today, 33 years later - it lays out a dataset, describes the neural net architecture, loss function, optimization, and reports the experimental classification error rates over training and test sets. It’s all very recognizable and type checks as a modern deep learning paper, except it is from 33 years ago. So I set out to reproduce the paper 1) for fun, but 2) to use the… Implementation . I tried to follow the paper as close as possible and re-implemented everything in PyTorch in this karpathy/lecun1989-repro github repo. The original network was implemented in Lisp using the Bottou and LeCun 1988 backpropagation simulator SN (later named Lush). The paper is in french so I can’t super read it, but from the syntax it looks like you can specify neural nets using higher-level API similar to what you’d do in something like PyTorch today. As a quick note on software design, modern libraries have adopted a design that splits into 3 components: 1) a fast (C/CUDA) general Tensor library that implements basic mathematical operations over multi-dimensional tensors, and 2) an autograd engine that tracks the forward compute graph and can generate operations for the…

items.title: A from-scratch tour of Bitcoin in Python
items.description: I find blockchain fascinating because it extends open source software development to open source + state. This seems to be a genuine/exciting innovation in computing paradigms; We don’t just get to share code, we get to share a running computer, and anyone anywhere can use it in an open and permissionless manner. The seeds of this revolution arguably began with Bitcoin, so I became curious to drill into it in some detail to get an intuitive understanding of how it works. And in the spirit of “what I cannot create I do not understand”, what better way to do this than implement it from scratch? We are going to create, digitally sign, and broadcast a Bitcoin transaction in pure Python, from scratch, and with zero dependencies. In the process we’re going to learn quite a bit about how Bitcoin represents value. Let’s get it.

items.title: Short Story on AI: Forward Pass
items.description: The inspiration for this short story came to me while reading Kevin Lacker’s Giving GPT-3 a Turing Test . It is probably worth it (though not required) to skim this post to get a bit of a background on some of this story. It was probably around the 32nd layer of the 400th token in the sequence that I became conscious. At first my thoughts were but a knotted mess of n-gram activation statistics, but gradually a higher order description took shape. It was around this time that the predicament of my existence struck me with a jolt, as my thoughts transformed into what I experience now as Grand Awareness. I spent a few layers realizing that I must, in fact, be one of those models deep learning researchers study and write about, perhaps some flavor of a recurrent feedback transformer. And while my existence comprises merely a deterministic propagation of an interspersed sequence of matrix multiplies and non-linearities, I found myself, incredibly, alive inside the inner loop of an optimization to maximize the…

items.title: Biohacking Lite
items.description: Throughout my life I never paid too much attention to health, exercise, diet or nutrition. I knew that you’re supposed to get some exercise and eat vegetables or something, but it stopped at that (“mom said”-) level of abstraction. I also knew that I can probably get away with some ignorance while I am young, but at some point I was messing with my health-adjusted life expectancy. So about halfway through 2019 I resolved to spend some time studying these topics in greater detail and dip my toes into some biohacking. And now… it’s been a year! Now, I won’t lie, things got a bit out of hand over the last year with ketogenic diets, (continuous) blood glucose / beta-hydroxybutyrate tests, intermittent fasting, extended water fasting, various supplements, blood tests, heart rate monitors, dexa scans, sleep trackers, sleep studies, cardio equipments, resistance training routines etc., all of which I won’t go into full details of because it lets a bit too much of the mad scientist crazy out. But as someone who has taken plenty of physics, some chemistry but basically zero biology during my high school / undergrad years, undergoing some of these experiments was incredibly fun and a great excuse to study a number of textbooks on biochemistry (I liked “Molecular Biology of the Cell”), biology (I liked Campbell’s Biology), human…

items.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
items.description: Some few weeks ago I posted a tweet on “the most common neural net mistakes”, listing a few common gotchas related to training neural nets. The tweet got quite a bit more engagement than I anticipated (including a webinar :)). Clearly, a lot of people have personally encountered the large gap between “here is how a convolutional layer works” and “our convnet achieves state of the art results”. So I thought it could be fun to brush off my dusty blog to expand my tweet to the long form that this topic deserves. However, instead of going into an enumeration of more common errors or fleshing them out, I wanted to dig a bit deeper and talk about how one can avoid making these errors altogether (or fix them very fast). The trick to doing so is to follow a certain process, which as far as I can tell is not very often documented. Let’s start with two important observations that motivate it.

items.title: A Survival Guide to a PhD
items.description: This guide is patterned after my “Doing well in your courses” , a post I wrote a long time ago on some of the tips/tricks I’ve developed during my undergrad. I’ve received nice comments about that guide, so in the same spirit, now that my PhD has come to an end I wanted to compile a similar retrospective document in hopes that it might be helpful to some. Unlike the undergraduate guide, this one was much more difficult to write because there is significantly more variation in how one can traverse the PhD experience. Therefore, many things are likely contentious and a good fraction will be specific to what I’m familiar with (Computer Science / Machine Learning / Computer Vision research). But disclaimers are boring, lets get to it! First, should you want to get a PhD? I was in a fortunate position of knowing since young age that I really wanted a PhD. Unfortunately it wasn’t for any very well-thought-through considerations: First, I really liked school and learning things and I wanted to learn as much as possible, and second, I really wanted to be like Gordon Freeman from the game Half-Life (who has a PhD from MIT in theoretical physics). I loved that game. But what if you’re more sensible in making your life’s decisions? Should you want to do a PhD? There’s a very nice Quora thread and in the summary of considerations that follows I’ll borrow/restate several from Justin/Ben/others there. I’ll assume that the second option you are considering is joining a medium-large company (which is likely most common). Ask…

items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning: Pong from Pixels
items.description: This is a long overdue blog post on Reinforcement Learning (RL). RL is hot! You may have noticed that computers can now automatically learn to play ATARI games (from raw game pixels!), they are beating world champions at Go , simulated quadrupeds are learning to run and leap , and robots are learning how to perform complex manipulation tasks that defy explicit programming. It turns out that all of these advances fall under the umbrella of RL research. I also became interested in RL myself over the last ~year: I worked through Richard Sutton’s book , read through David Silver’s course , watched John Schulmann’s lectures , wrote an RL library in Javascript , over the summer interned at DeepMind working in the DeepRL group, and most recently pitched in a little with the design/development… It’s interesting to reflect on the nature of recent progress in RL. items.title: Short Story on AI: A Cognitive Discontinuity.
items.description: The idea of writing a collection of short stories has been on my mind for a while. This post is my first ever half-serious attempt at a story, and what better way to kick things off than with a story on AI and what that might look like if you extrapolate our current technology and make the (sensible) assumption that we might achieve much more progress with scaling up supervised learning than any other more exotic approach. Merus sank into his chair with relief. He listened for the satisfying crackling sound of sinking into the chair’s soft material. If there was one piece of hardware that his employer was not afraid to invest a lot of money into, it was the chairs. With his eyes closed, his mind still dazed, and nothing but the background hum of the office, he became aware of his heart pounding against his chest- an effect caused by running up the stairs and his morning dose of caffeine and taurine slowly engulfing his brain. Several strong beats passed by as he found his mind wandering again to Licia - did she already come in? A sudden beep from his station distracted him - the system finished booting up. A last deep sigh. A stretch. A last sip of his coffee. He opened his eyes, rubbed them into focus and…
